title: Motion to Intervene and Comments of the Data Center Coalition re Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.'s 08/28/2026 filing under ER26-3650.

documents.name: DCC Comments - MISO IRR Filing.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )
Midcontinent Independent System                        )                   Docket No. ER26-3650-000
Operator, Inc.                                         )


                            MOTION TO INTERVENE
                  AND COMMENTS OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”) 1 and the Commission’s August 31, 2026

Combined Notice of Filings #1, 2 the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) hereby moves to intervene

and submits these comments on Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“MISO”)

proposal to establish certain Interconnection Reliability Requirements (“IRR”) for large loads. 3

I.      OVERVIEW OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

        DCC is the membership organization for the U.S. data center industry, representing leading

data center owners and operators that develop, operate, and maintain data center infrastructure and

teams across the country. 4 DCC members operate data centers that constitute significant loads

within the MISO region and DCC has been an active stakeholder in regional efforts to ensure

reliability, enable new generation, and discipline load forecasts. DCC and its members have been

at the forefront of efforts to advance reforms in MISO and at the state level to accommodate the

           18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.214.
        2
           Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., et al., Docket No. ER26-3650-000, et al., Combined
Notice of Filings #1 (Aug. 31, 2026).
         3
           Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER26-3650-000, Proposal of Midcontinent
Independent System Operator, Inc. to Establish Certain Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads

written comments submitted by DCC do not necessarily reflect the views of each individual DCC member. A list of

 growth of large loads within the MISO region while maintaining reliability and protecting existing

retail customers.

II.        INTRODUCTION

           DCC appreciates MISO’s continued proactive engagement with the data center industry,

and its efforts to develop reliability requirements that facilitate the integration of large loads while

preserving the reliable operation of the transmission system. DCC member facilities depend upon

reliable electricity service, and DCC shares MISO’s objective of ensuring that the interconnection

and operation of large load customers does not adversely affect reliability, system operations, or

other customers. DCC recognizes that large loads may present operational characteristics that

warrant distinct reliability requirements and standards to maintain transmission system reliability.

DCC is committed to working collaboratively with MISO, the North American Electric Reliability

Corporation (“NERC”), and stakeholders to establish requirements that maintain reliability,

protect customers, and avoid creating barriers to large load growth.

           The issue presented by MISO’s Filing is not whether transmission customers taking service

for large loads should be subject to distinct visibility and operational requirements.                            The

Commission already resolved this issue in its June 2026 show cause order finding the MISO tariff

unjust and unreasonable because it does not include provisions establishing ride-through, ramping,

and other operational requirements to address the challenges of large load integration. 5 Instead,

the issue is whether the framework that MISO has proposed in this proceeding represents a just

and reasonable means of mitigating these reliability risks. While DCC appreciates MISO’s efforts

to develop a compliance framework and recognizes the difficulty of the task, DCC respectfully




           5
               Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., et al., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at PP 43, 64 (2026) (“Show Cause
Order”).


                                                           -2-
 submits that MISO’s proposal, as filed, falls short of the clear and consistent framework that the

Show Cause Order contemplated.

         One of the primary objectives of the Show Cause Order is to ensure that the MISO tariff

includes clear rules governing the provision of transmission service to customers serving large

loads “to ensure regulatory and process certainty, fairness and consistency, and efficiency as large

and co-located loads are added to the transmission system[.]” 6 Indeed, MISO has acknowledged

the need for reform, stating that its “existing Tariff provisions ‘do not provide a consistent or

transparent framework to evaluate’ large loads and that interested parties ‘face uncertainty

regarding applicable criteria, study assumptions, data requirements, and post-interconnection

obligations.’” 7 DCC agrees with that assessment—and it is precisely because DCC shares MISO’s

diagnosis of the problem—that it believes that MISO’s tariff revisions must go farther to establish

the types of “clear and consistent” tariff provisions contemplated by the Commission. 8

         MISO has not demonstrated that the framework that MISO has proposed would resolve the

uncertainty, consistency, or transparency issues identified in the Show Cause Order. MISO

proposes to revise its tariff to provide itself with new authority to impose new visibility and

reliability requirements on Large Loads and Computational Loads. But the proposed tariff

revisions do not clearly define the customers that will be subject to those requirements and the

obligations that will apply. Instead, MISO proposes to include the substance of the reliability

requirements in a future Business Practices Manual (“BPM”). The result is a tariff framework that




         6
            Id. at P 12.
         7
            Id. at P 29 (quoting MISO, Issue Submission Report (Apr. 15, 2026), available at:
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/New%20Issue%20-
%20Large%20Load%20Interconnection%20Reliability%20Requirements748710.pdf).
          8
            Id. at PP 12, 61, 64, 126.


                                                        -3-
 fails to deliver the regulatory certainty, consistency, and notice required by the Show Cause Order

and the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).

       MISO’s proposed grandfathering framework suffers from similar issues. Although the

Commission directed MISO to minimize disruption to existing commercial arrangements, MISO

ties grandfathered treatment primarily to whether an associated transmission project has reached

specified milestones in the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) or Expedited Project

Review (“EPR”) rather than to whether the Large Load customer has entered into binding

agreements or made material investments in reliance on the existing regulatory framework. The

result is a grandfathering framework that is disconnected from the commercial arrangements that

the Commission sought to preserve in the Show Cause Order. 9 Additionally, MISO has proposed

to grant itself broad discretion to subject customers that otherwise qualify for an exemption to its

reliability standards without including any objective standards or procedures in the tariff, creating

uncertainty about whether customers will be exempt from these requirements or whether MISO

may later withdraw that protection.

       DCC is not opposed to efforts by MISO or other transmission providers to impose

reliability requirements necessary to account for the operational characteristics of large loads.

Maintaining grid reliability is a top priority for DCC and its members. If MISO demonstrates that

new reliability requirements are necessary to mitigate reliability risks, then the MISO tariff should

be modified to include the necessary safeguards to ensure that transmission customers install

equipment and abide by operational limitations needed to maintain reliability.

       However, any reliability framework that is implemented should be objective, transparent,

and provide clear notice to customers of the scope of their obligations and the steps needed to



       9
           See id. at PP 5, 36.


                                                -4-
 comply with such requirements, with appropriate measures to minimize disruption to existing

commercial arrangements and reasonable implementation periods. Customers must have clarity

on their compliance obligations so they can make the design decisions necessary to meet these

obligations. At the same time, it is important to recognize that customers with facilities that are

under development or that have commenced operation may not be able to easily revisit investment

and design decisions without incurring significant delays and costs. Reliability requirements

should be implemented in a manner that respects settled expectations and avoids unnecessary

disruption to existing investment decisions to the extent consistent with the objective of

maintaining reliability.

       Thus, while DCC supports the critically important reliability imperatives underlying

MISO’s Filing, DCC respectfully requests that the Commission decline to accept MISO’s

proposed tariff revisions as filed, without prejudice to a future filing that proposes implementation

of new reliability requirements in a manner that is objective, transparent, and consistent with the

objectives of the Show Cause Order. Although DCC believes that the Filing should be rejected,

DCC encourages MISO to work with the region to further refine and clarify its proposals and

identify a path forward that provides the certainty and durability needed to effectively ensure that

large loads take the steps and make the investments necessary to meet the reliability imperatives

that MISO rightly aims to safeguard.




                                                -5-
 III.     COMMENTS

         A.        MISO’s Filing Is Inconsistent With The Show Cause Order, The FPA, And
                   The Rule Of Reason

                   1.       MISO’s Proposal To Relegate The Substance Of Its Requirements To
                            Its BPMs Is Inconsistent With The FPA

         Section 205 of the FPA requires public utilities to file the rates, terms, and conditions of

FERC-jurisdictional service with the Commission. 10 This obligation includes “classifications,

practices, and regulations affecting such rates and charges[.]” 11 Additionally, “no change shall be

made” in any rate, term, condition, or practice without a Section 205 filing providing notice of the

change to the Commission and the public, and only after the Commission determines that the

change is just and reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. 12 These basic

statutory requirements are reflected in the Filed Rate Doctrine, which prohibits public utilities from

imposing any rates, terms, and conditions other than those that have been filed with and approved

by the Commission.13

         Section 205 and the Filed Rate Doctrine are designed to ensure that customers receive

advance notice of the rates, terms, and conditions of service and the Commission can exercise its

authority necessary to maintain just and reasonable rates. 14 As the courts have recognized, the




         10
            16 U.S.C. § 824d.
         11
            Id.; see also 18 C.F.R. § 35.1(a) (requiring that any “rates and charges . . . classifications, practices, rules
and regulations affecting such rates, charges, classifications, services, rules, regulations or practices,” be filed).
         12
            16 U.S.C. § 824d(d).
         13
            See Ark. La. Gas Co. v. Hall, 453 U.S. 571, 577 (1981) (stating that the filed rate doctrine “forbids a
regulated entity to charge rates for its services other than those properly filed with the appropriate federal regulatory
authority”) (“Arkansas Louisiana Gas”).
         14
            Cogentrix Energy Power Mgmt., LLC v. FERC, 24 F.4th 677, 683 (D.C. Cir. 2022); see also Town of
Concord v. FERC, 955 F.2d 67, 71 (D.C. Cir. 1992) (explaining that purpose of filed rate doctrine is “preservation of
the agency’s primary jurisdiction over reasonableness of rates and the need to insure that regulated companies charge
only those rates of which the agency has been made cognizant”) (quoting Arkansas Louisiana Gas at 577-578).


                                                           -6-
 requirement “of transparent, public filing of rates ensures evenhandedness, fairness, stability, and

predictability” in the rates charged for FERC-jurisdictional service. 15

        But the FPA and Filed Rate Doctrine are not satisfied merely because a public utility has

filed a tariff with FERC. The FPA, FERC’s regulations, and the Filed Rate Doctrine require that

the tariff “clearly and specifically” set forth the rates, terms, and conditions, and practices affecting

such rates, terms, and conditions, of FERC-jurisdictional service. 16 A tariff that omits key terms

and conditions of service in favor of vague or open-ended references to a public utility’s

procedures and practices is inconsistent with the FPA and the Filed Rate Doctrine, and ultimately

unjust and unreasonable. 17

        MISO’s proposed tariff revisions do not satisfy these requirements. While DCC recognizes

that not every ministerial implementation detail must be included in the tariff, MISO’s tariff

revisions do not include the substantive standards that MISO proposes to apply, leave key aspects

of MISO’s proposed framework unaddressed, and grant MISO broad discretion to apply the

standards to customers as it deems appropriate without any objective requirements to constrain

this discretion. Instead, the tariff repeatedly defers the substance of these standards and key aspects

of how these standards will be applied to a new Large Load BPM that remains under development

by MISO, including the performance standards and limits that customers will be held to, 18 testing

requirements and other procedures for demonstrating compliance with MISO’s standards, and the

timelines for providing required information to MISO. 19 The result is a tariff framework that

        16
             Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 182 FERC ¶ 61,100, at P 34 (2023) (“SPP Order”). See also 18 C.F.R. § 35.1(a)
(stating that tariffs must “clearly and specifically” set out rates, charges, and practices for FERC-jurisdictional
service).
          17
             Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC v. FERC, 474 F.3d 804, 810-11 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (“Keyspan-Ravenswood”).
          18
             Filing, Tab A, Proposed §§ 37A.6, 37A.7.
          19
             Id., Proposed § 37A.1.


                                                       -7-
 informs customers that they will be subject to ride-through requirements, ramp-rate limitations,

and other requirements, but leaves customers in the dark about the substance of their compliance

obligations.

         The Commission’s Rule of Reason does not justify MISO’s decision to leave the substance

of its proposed requirements to the BPMs. Instead, the Commission’s Rule of Reason requires

public utilities to file those practices or provisions that “significantly affect rates and services”20

while permitting only implementation details of “practical insignificance” 21 to be included in

BPMs or other manuals. The Rule of Reason requires terms and conditions to be included in the

tariff if they “affect rates and services significantly, . . . are realistically susceptible of specification,

. . . are not so generally understood . . . as to render recitation superfluous,” 22 and are not “clearly

implied by the tariff’s express terms.” 23 Rather than supporting MISO’s proposal, applying the

Rule of Reason to the tariff provisions that MISO has filed in this proceeding highlights the

problems with MISO’s approach.

                          i.         The Tariff Must Include The Reliability Standards That
                                     Customers Will Be Required To Meet

         MISO proposes to require that a transmission customer taking service on behalf of a

Computational Load comply with ramping limits and ride-through requirements. Although MISO

notes in its transmittal letter that it is considering an initial limit of 30 MW/minute, MISO does

not propose to include the actual limits and requirements in the tariff. 24 For instance, MISO’s


         20
            See, e.g., Boston Energy Trading & Mktg. LLC v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 153 FERC ¶
61,336, at P 39 (2015).
         21
            Pub. Serv. Comm’n of N.Y. v. FERC, 813 F.2d 448, 454 (D.C. Cir. 1987) (holding that the Commission
properly excused utilities from filing policies or practices that dealt with only matters of “practical insignificance” to
serving customers).
         22
            Id. (quoting City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985)).
         23
            Cometa Energia, S.A. de C.V. v. Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 191 FERC ¶ 61,089, at PP 10, 19
(2025), order on reh’g, 193 FERC ¶ 61,011 (2025).
         24
            Filing, Tab A, Proposed § 37A.7.


                                                          -8-
 tariff revisions state that Computational Load will be subject to “up-ramp and down-ramp limits

established by [MISO]” and must have “an effective up and down ramp rate not exceeding the

specified limit,” but the tariff does not specify the actual limits that will apply, the procedures that

will be used to determine the applicable limits, or how MISO will determine a load’s “effective”

ramp rate. 25 Similarly, MISO’s proposed ride-through requirements state that Computational Load

must remain connected to the transmission system and continue to operate during voltage and

frequency disturbances within the “performance criteria” established by MISO, but does not

provide any detail regarding the performance criteria that will be applied. 26 The tariff also states

that the ride-through requirements “may include evaluation, testing, modeling, monitoring, and

other compliance measures,” but states that these measures will be detailed in MISO’s BPMs. 27

        MISO has not demonstrated that excluding the substance of these requirements from the

tariff is just, reasonable, and consistent with the FPA. There is little question that the ramp rate

and ride-through requirements applied to transmission customers serving Large Loads

significantly affect the rates, terms, and conditions of FERC-jurisdictional service.                     The

Commission recognized as much in the Show Cause Order by directing MISO to include ramp

rate and ride-through requirements in its tariff. 28 Additionally, compliance with MISO’s proposed

ramp rate and ride-through requirements is a precondition to receiving service, and failure to abide

by these requirements may lead MISO to delay or limit the availability of service.

        Likewise, there is little question that these requirements are readily susceptible to

specification. Indeed, MISO states that it plans to impose an initial limit of 30 MW per minute,

           Id.
        26

        27

        28
           Show Cause Order at P 64 (stating that absence of tariff provisions addressing ramp and ride-through
requirements may lead to unjust and unreasonable rates).


                                                     -9-
 demonstrating that the limit is both known and realistically susceptible to specification. 29 Both

the Commission and the courts have recognized that numerical thresholds, such as the ramp limit,

are “susceptible of specification” and should be included in the tariff. 30 Similarly, MISO already

has published a technical compendium describing its proposed ride-through requirements,

including minimum ride-through times, 31 and the MISO tariff has long included ride-through

requirements for generation resources. 32 Neither the proposed ramp rate nor the ride-through

requirements are generally understood or implied by the tariff’s express terms, as there is no set of

standard “ramp rates” or “ride-through” requirements that are applicable and nothing in the

proposed terms of the tariff implies a specific ramp limitation or ride-through requirement.

         Also, the procedures and protocols that are used by MISO to verify a transmission

customer’s compliance with these requirements significantly affect the rates, terms, and conditions

of service and should be described in the tariff. The Commission has found that the tariff should

describe procedures that are used to measure and verify compliance with tariff requirements. 33

Indeed, the MISO tariff includes detailed provisions describing how MISO evaluates compliance

with operational restrictions for other resource and customer classes, including the frequency of

testing, the nature of the tests that will be administered, applicable performance standards,

requires be stated in the [t]ariff, as a numerical threshold is ‘realistically susceptible of specification.’” (quoting

             Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 137 FERC ¶ 61,214, at P 79 (2011) (directing MISO to

                                                        - 10 -
 procedures for seeking waivers, and other pertinent details. 34 DCC is not arguing that every

ministerial detail of MISO’s proposed compliance procedures need to be included in the tariff. But

transmission customers serving Large Load customers should be given a level of certainty and

transparency that is comparable to that regularly afforded to other customers and market

participants.

                        ii.        The Terms And Conditions Of “Ramp Smoothing” Must Be In
                                   The Tariff

         MISO proposes to allow customers to comply with the ramp requirements using

“reduction/ramp smoothing provided by generation or other resources that meet[] the eligibility

requirements specified in” the BPM for Large Load. 35 Absent from the proposed tariff, however,

is any description of how ramp smoothing would affect ramp limits, what resources would be

eligible to provide this service, or how resource contributions would be measured and accounted

for in the effective ramp rate. In fact, neither the transmittal letter nor the testimony submitted in

support of MISO’s filing provides any detail about this ramp smoothing “service” or how it would

figure into a customer’s ramp limitations.

         The terms and conditions of ramp smoothing must be included in the tariff. The eligibility

requirements to provide ramp smoothing, the methodology used to measure a resource’s

contribution, and the extent to which these contributions may offset a customer’s ramp limitations

significantly affect rates, as these requirements will dictate the ability of resources to provide ramp

smoothing and whether a customer will be deemed to have met applicable compliance




         34
             MISO Tariff, § 69.A.3.5(j) (stating that market participant must demonstrate demand reduction capability
by performing annual test, testing conditions, procedures for obtaining waiver from these requirements, and the
performance standards that must be demonstrated during the test); id. §§ 1F, 40.2.5 (describing testing requirements
for fast ramping resources, including applicable performance standards and consequences of non-compliance).
          35
             Filing, Tab A, Proposed § 37A.7.


                                                       - 11 -
 obligations. 36 Additionally, the requirements governing ramp smoothing are readily susceptible

to specification, as MISO could easily identify the categories of eligible resources, the performance

criteria applicable to these resources, and the methodology used to calculate the contribution of

these resources to meeting ramping requirements, as MISO already does for other services and

products that are traded within the MISO markets. 37 Nor are the requirements associated with

ramp smoothing reasonably implied by, or otherwise apparent from, the tariff itself.

                        iii.        The Tariff Must Include Objective Standards And Procedures
                                    For Revoking Exemptions

         The problems with MISO’s approach are not limited to the substance of the reliability

requirements that MISO proposes to apply to customers. While MISO proposes to include

grandfathering criteria in its tariff, MISO also proposes to grant itself authority to require an

otherwise exempt customer to comply with its proposed reliability requirements whenever it

“determines that operation of a Large Load results in a material adverse effect on Transmission

System reliability.” 38 MISO’s proposed tariff language does not describe the criteria that it would

apply to revoke a customer’s exemption, any rights to appeal or challenge this determination, the

process that it would use to require compliance with these standards, or the transition period that

would be provided for a customer to bring itself into compliance. Instead, the tariff states that

            See, e.g., Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 169 FERC ¶ 61,048, at P 62 (2019) (finding that four-hour minimum-run-
time requirement significantly affects rates because it determined eligibility of resources to satisfy resource adequacy
requirements).
         37
            See, e.g., MISO Tariff, §§ 39.2.1A(f)(i)-(ii), 39.2.1B(D), 40.2.4(d).
         38
            Filing, Tab A, Proposed § 37A(II)(3).


                                                        - 12 -
 “[t]he process by which [MISO] will make such a determination and which, if any, of the

requirements of . . . Section 37A are to be applied” will be included in the BPM for Large Load. 39

       The criteria and process used by MISO to make the extraordinary decision to revoke an

exemption conferred by the express terms of the tariff will have a significant effect on the

transmission service provided to customers serving Large Loads. A determination by MISO to

revoke a customer’s exemption would fundamentally change the operational requirements that

would apply to a transmission customer and the associated Large Load. Additionally, the criteria

MISO applies when evaluating whether to revoke an exemption will determine whether revocation

is reserved for extraordinary circumstances or may occur as a matter of course. Equally important,

the timing of any such evaluation and the compliance timeline afforded to an affected customer

will determine whether revocation is a manageable transition or a significant disruption to the

customer’s operations.

       Additionally, without tariff provisions that clearly set out the standards and procedures

governing revocation, the Commission cannot meaningfully evaluate whether MISO’s proposed

grandfathering framework will achieve the objective of minimizing disruption to existing

commercial arrangements. The practical effect is that the Commission is being asked to approve

a framework for protecting settled expectations without knowing the criteria under which those

protections may be withdrawn.

       There is no reason that MISO cannot describe the standards and processes that it would use

to revoke an exemption in the tariff—just as it has described the criteria that customers would be

required to meet to qualify for an exemption in the first place. And nothing about MISO’s




       39
            Id.


                                              - 13 -
 process—from the standards applied to how MISO would implement this authority—is generally

understood or implied by the limited description that MISO has proposed to include in the tariff.

                          iv.     MISO Has Not Justified The Omission Of Metering Standards
                                  And Other Requirements

         MISO’s proposed tariff language also omits other significant requirements related to the

standards and procedures that will be applied to transmission customers and the Large Loads that

they serve. For instance, while the Commission has recognized that the Rule of Reason requires

metering standards to be described in the tariff and the existing tariff already includes detailed

metering requirements for market participants, 40 MISO’s proposed tariff revisions in this

proceeding do not provide any detail about the metering standards that will be applied to Large

Load or any generation resources serving these customers. 41 The Commission also has found that

procedural deadlines, such as deadlines for submitting data and information to a transmission

provider, should be specified in the tariff, particularly where the failure to abide by these

requirements could have adverse consequences for entities taking service under the tariff. 42 Yet,

MISO again proposes to leave such deadlines to its BPMs even though failure to comply with

these requirements may adversely affect a customer’s ability to receive transmission service. 43

         The matters described above may not be as consequential as the criteria used to determine

whether to revoke an exemption from tariff requirements or the substance of the reliability

including applicable minimum standards, accuracy standards, and testing requirements).

          42

 standards that MISO proposes to apply.         But they nonetheless significantly affect FERC-

jurisdictional service as transmission customers and the Large Loads that they serve must comply

with these requirements to obtain service. They also are the types of details that are regularly

included in transmission provider tariffs. MISO has not demonstrated that providing transmission

customers serving Large Loads and their customers with less notice and transparency than other

customers is just, reasonable, and consistent with the Rule of Reason.

                       v.   MISO’s Approach Undermines Certainty, Predictability, And
                            Commission Oversight

       The practical effect of the tariff revisions that have been proposed is that neither the

Commission nor commenters have the information necessary to determine whether the substance

of MISO’s proposed framework is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

This places the Commission and commenters in the impossible position of being asked to evaluate

a reliability framework without any insight into the substance of the standards or other key terms

and conditions of service. Without the operative standards and procedures before it, the

Commission cannot determine whether the proposed requirements are supported by demonstrated

reliability needs, reasonably tailored to the risks MISO seeks to address, capable of being applied

consistently to similarly situated customers, or will achieve the objective of minimizing disruption

to existing commercial arrangements.

       MISO’s proposed framework undermines the certainty that the Show Cause Order sought

to promote.    The proposed tariff language does not provide customers with notice of the

requirements that will apply, how compliance will be assessed, or even whether their facilities

ultimately will be deemed subject to these requirements. Large Load customers need to understand

the scope of their obligations when making investment decisions and entering commercial

arrangements. And the tariff must provide customers with assurance that exemptions, once



                                               - 15 -
 granted, cannot be summarily revoked based on a subjective MISO assessment without regard to

the stage of development of their facilities.

       MISO’s proposal also creates a risk of inconsistent standards and application.

Transmission customers serving Large Loads or Computational Loads should be subject to a

common set of standards and requirements, as applicable.          Yet, since the details of these

requirements are not provided in the tariff, neither the Commission nor customers have any

assurance that the requirements that ultimately are adopted will be applied in a manner that ensures

consistent and non-discriminatory treatment of customers.

       Finally, the proposed framework would allow MISO to create through future BPM

revisions the very disruption to settled expectations that the Show Cause Order directed MISO to

avoid. Placing the substance of MISO’s reliability requirements in the BPMs means that the

standards, as well as their application to individual customers, can be modified by MISO without

formal notice to customers or approval by the Commission. As the Commission recognized in the

Show Cause Order, the application of new reliability requirements to customers has the potential

to disrupt the settled expectations of customers that have relied on existing market rules when

developing their facilities. 44 It was precisely for this reason that the Commission directed MISO

to propose measures to minimize disruption to existing commercial arrangements. 45 Yet, MISO’s

proposal would allow it to revise these same requirements through the BPMs after customers have

designed their facilities and entered commercial arrangements without making a Section 205 filing

or seeking Commission approval—and without any obligation to take steps to protect settled

expectations.




       44
            Show Cause Order at P 123.
       45
            Id.

        B.          MISO Has Not Demonstrated That Its Proposed Definition Of Large Load Is
                   Just, Reasonable, And Not Unduly Discriminatory Or Preferential

       MISO’s proposed definition of Large Load also creates ambiguity regarding the scope and

application of MISO’s proposed requirements. Because classification as a “Large Load” carries
